summary:
We developed Agro Field, a Next.js and FastAPI web application that helps Ugandan farmers explore crop rotations. It combines locally stored NASA-derived rainfall, temperature and modelled soil wetness with crop references, soil information and farmer priorities.

Users select a sample area on an interactive map, view historical graphs and enter crop plans. The tool compares their existing rotation with reference-based alternatives, explains evidence gaps and exports a PDF report.

Agro Field connects Earth observations with farming decisions as changing rainfall, water shortages and declining soil health make planning harder. It makes environmental evidence easier to understand and supports discussions about soil health and climate resilience. Local review guides final decisions.
details:
What we developed

Agro Field is a web application that helps Ugandan farmers explore crop-rotation options using environmental evidence and their own priorities. It brings an interactive map, historical graphs, crop comparisons and downloadable reports into one workspace.

How it works

Users choose one of four sample areas nearGulu (Northern Uganda), Mbale (Eastern Uganda), Masaka (Central Uganda), or Mbarara (Western Uganda). They can explore rainfall, temperature and modelled soil wetness from 2016–2025, then enter their crop history, planned crops, water supply and priorities.

The application combines locally stored NASA-derived records with FAO crop references and soil information. Farmers can enter measured soil pH or use a clearly labelled area estimate.

For supported crops, the tool compares the farmer’s existing plan with up to two alternatives. It checks crop preferences, exclusions, soil pH, available growing days and historical temperature against saved crop ranges. Results explain the checks, identify missing evidence and provide a PDF report.

Benefits and intended impact

Agro Field makes environmental information easier to understand through maps, graphs and simple explanations. Keeping the existing rotation visible helps farmers compare options while retaining their own starting plan.

The intended impact is better-informed crop planning and more useful conversations between farmers and agricultural advisers. The project supports discussions about water conditions, soil health and adapting to changing weather. Improvements in yield, income or water savings would need future field testing.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS and shadcn-style components.
  • Forms and state: React Hook Form, Zod, nuqs and Zustand.
  • Charts and animation: Recharts and Motion.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Pydantic and pandas, served with Uvicorn.
  • PDF reports: Matplotlib and ReportLab, using DM Sans.
  • Development: GitHub repositories with separate development stages.

The prototype reads downloaded files during normal analysis, reducing dependence on live data services.

What makes it creative

Agro Field connects past environmental conditions with the farmer’s next crop-planning discussion. Users can replay historical periods, inspect the evidence behind individual checks and carry the same information into a report. Its creativity lies in making several technical resources understandable within a simple farming workflow.

What we considered

The design considers clear English, phone screens, readable controls and slower connections. It also considers Uganda’s crop choices and the different needs of seasonal and long-lived crops such as coffee.

Data limits remain visible. Satellite and model estimates describe conditions around sample points, while field measurements provide more specific information. Crop-range checks provide starting points for local review; they do not establish the benefits of an entire rotation.
